title: Offline update runbook discussion - AxiomPath Medical
summary: Introductory discovery on air-gapped update/runbook process, hardware constraints, and governance needs for a private Redwood deployment. Customer wants a clear signed-update flow, validation gates, and maintenance windows before committing to on-prem Private. Next steps include runbook template, security whitepaper, and an on-site hardware survey.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-12 15:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Dr. Lina Ortiz, Markus Lee, Priya Shah, Evan Torres

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. i'm jordan patel from redwood, i'm the account lead. maya is our solutions engineer. could we do a quick round of intros and what you want to get out of this session?
[00:07] Dr. Lina Ortiz: sure, i'm lina, cto at axiompath. main thing for us is to understand how updates work in an air-gapped environment — we can't have any outbound egress. we need to know how models and runtime patches are delivered and validated.
[00:22] Markus Lee: hi, markus. my team actually runs the datacenter and, yea, our procurement cycle is slow so we need a runbook that maps to our change windows. also curious about hardware: we currently have a mix of two A100 gen1 and several older V100s.
[00:36] Priya Shah: priya from compliance — SOC2 in scope, but we also have regional data residency and need audit trails for model changes. we need to understand what audit logs exist and how to link them to our SIEM.
[00:49] Maya: thanks all. quick framing: we support three deployment modes but sounds like you're evaluating private offline deployment. today we'll focus on update flow, verification, and what tooling we hand over. i'll share some examples of signed bundles and validation steps.
[01:05] Jordan: and we'll be candid about tradeoffs — e.g., frequent model updates vs. stability, and whether you want Redwood-managed artifacts shipped via signed images or prefer to bake artifacts yourself.
[01:16] Dr. Lina Ortiz: can you walk through a typical "air-gapped update" end-to-end? like who signs what, and how do we verify?
[01:24] Maya: yeah absolutely. so our recommended pattern is: 1) we produce a release bundle that includes model weights (optionally quantized), runtime binaries, and a manifest. 2) the bundle is signed by a Redwood release key (or by your key if you want). 3) you transfer the bundle into the isolated environment via secure removable media or a controlled transfer node. 4) pre-deploy validation runs — checksums, signature verification, small smoke tests against a canned prompt set. 5) staged rollout within cluster with KV cache priming and a canary pool. 6) monitoring and rollback policy.
[02:10] Evan Torres: small question — when you say "signed by a Redwood release key or your key" what's the expected flow if we want to use our HSM?
[02:16] Maya: good question. we support two flows: a) we sign artifacts and provide the public verification key that you import into your HSM/verifier, or b) we provide unsigned artifacts and a reproducible build manifest so you can sign with your HSM before import. many customers choose option b for regulated workloads.
[02:35] Markus Lee: also, do you provide a way to roll forward patches on older GPU hardware? our V100s are slower, memory is constrained. can the runtime degrade gracefully or do we need separate quantized model builds?
[02:46] Maya: runtime supports quantized variants and smaller cache configurations. for older cards we recommend a quantized model variant and a smaller max batch size. we can also produce a model variant compiled for the target compute capabilities — that is part of the offline delivery if you want.
[03:05] Priya Shah: auditability — where are logs persisted? we don't want any telemetry leaving the environment.
[03:10] Jordan: all telemetry is optional. for private/offline, we provide an on-prem console that writes logs locally to a pluggable sink; you can ship to your SIEM with syslog or file forwarders. we also provide an offline archive format for token-level cost and inference traces that you can ingest later.
[03:27] Priya Shah: ok good. is that FIPS or HSM-ready for key wrapping?
[03:31] Maya: yes we support KMS integrations — for offline we have an HSM adapter that maps to PKCS#11. we don't ship keys out; key operations can be constrained to the device.
[03:40] Dr. Lina Ortiz: what's the smallest maintenance window we can expect? our clinical batch windows are narrow — maybe 1 hour at night.
[03:47] Jordan: depends on update size and tests. for a minor runtime patch with pre-cached KV and a small smoke test, target ~30-45 minutes. for model swaps it's typically longer — 1.5 to 3 hours depending on priming, unless you pre-seed caches during an earlier prep window.
[04:04] Markus Lee: hmm, 1.5 to 3 hours for model swap could be tough. can we do partial rollouts so only a small pool gets the model first while others continue?
[04:11] Maya: yes canary pools are the recommended approach. you can route a low percentage of traffic to the canary and validate outputs against a prompt suite. if results are good, you expand the pool. this reduces blast radius and shortens perceived downtime.
[04:26] Evan Torres: about validations — do you provide an eval harness? our team needs reproducible tests for NLU regressions.
[04:32] Maya: we have a small eval harness for offline use — a dockerized runner with a test prompt set and a diff tool. we can ship it as part of the bundle or as a separate artifact. it's intentionally minimal to run inside isolated environments.
[04:45] Priya Shah: incident response — if a model produces bad outputs mid-shift, how fast can we rollback?
[04:51] Jordan: rollback is a single command to redeploy the previous artifact in the manifest; with canaries, you can detect issues before full rollout. realistic rollback time is similar to rollout time but smaller if artifacts are cached locally. also we can provide automated failover to a smaller model variant that is on all nodes to keep latency stable.
[05:10] Dr. Lina Ortiz: curious about signature verification process — are signatures retained in manifests and are they timestamped? we need chain-of-custody for audits.
[05:20] Maya: manifests include signature metadata, signer id, timestamp, and hash of included artifacts. we also produce a human-readable release note that you can store alongside the artifact for audits.
[05:30] Markus Lee: can you talk about physical transfer recommendations? we currently have strict transfer stations and an approved stamping process for media.
[05:37] Maya: we recommend controlled transfer via an intermediate staging host in a DMZ that your team controls. after transfer you should checksum and verify signature before ingestion. for very sensitive customers, we also support an encrypted bundle with keys provisioned via your HSM.
[05:55] Evan Torres: do you support delta updates vs full rebuilds? we want to avoid shipping huge models every time.
[06:00] Maya: delta support is limited because model weights are large; we do provide quantized diffs in some cases and a delta manifest that tells the runtime how to patch weights. for larger model changes, a full bundle is more common. we'll discuss specifics in a followup RWK (runbook).
[06:18] Jordan: quick pause — priority for axiompath is compliance and predictable ops. cost/latency tradeoffs are secondary to stability here, correct?
[06:26] Dr. Lina Ortiz: yes, we need deterministic validation and an audit trail. cost is secondary.
[06:30] Maya: noted. on the encryption front, we can do disk-level encryption, model-level encryption, and wrap keys with your HSM. logs never leave unless you opt-in.
[06:42] Priya Shah: do you have SSO and RBAC hooks for the on-prem console?
[06:46] Maya: yes SAML/SSO is supported and you can map roles to RBAC policies. we also provide an admin audit log for actions like deploy, rollback, signature-verify.
[06:58] Markus Lee: procurement note — our facilities team will want a BOM (bill of materials) with recommended GPUs and expected throughput for a given SLA. can you provide a sizing guide?
[07:06] Jordan: yes, we have a throughput matrix that maps model family, batch size, and GPU types to RPS and latency medians. we'll attach a preliminary sizing doc.
[07:16] Dr. Lina Ortiz: how do you handle model lineage? we need to tie a specific model to training data version and evals as part of the audit record.
[07:24] Maya: we include metadata in the manifest for model lineage — training hash, dataset id, eval snapshot. for private deployments you can require that metadata be present and assert checks during verification.
[07:36] Evan Torres: any example of a runbook we can see?
[07:40] Jordan: we'll share a sanitized runbook that reflects a standard update flow — step-by-step transfer, verification commands, smoke tests, common rollback commands, and owner escalation contacts.
[07:52] Priya Shah: what about emergency hotfixes — can you provide a signed hotfix outside normal cadence?
[07:58] Maya: yes we have an expedited release process. hotfixes are signed and we provide a separate manifest path; you still need to verify signatures. for maximum speed we can coordinate a pre-authorized approval list so your ops team can accept hotfixes faster.
[08:12] Dr. Lina Ortiz: can we sandbox a release first in an isolated test cluster that mirrors production?
[08:17] Maya: absolutely, that's best practice. we recommend a mirrored test cluster where you first deploy to a node pool with traffic replay from a captured traffic set. run the eval harness, compare results, then schedule cutover.
[08:30] Markus Lee: a couple of practical questions — how big are signed bundles typically? and what's the suggested transfer mechanism for our network with 1Gb egress to staging?
[08:38] Maya: bundles vary — a full FP16 model bundle with runtime can be multiple hundreds of gigabytes. quantized or trimmed variants can be tens of gigabytes. for constrained links we support shipping encrypted disk images via courier or using an intermediate transfer appliance.
[08:55] Evan Torres: about monitoring — you mentioned local observability. does the console have token-level cost breakdowns in the offline mode?
[09:02] Jordan: yes we generate token and invocation-level metrics locally. the console exposes similar views to hosted, but data is stored in your cluster. you can export csvs to your finance tooling.
[09:15] Priya Shah: auditing again — do you support immutable logs (WORM) for compliance?
[09:19] Maya: we support immutable append-only log snapshots that you can export and store in your compliance storage. it's part of the audit bundle.
[09:28] Dr. Lina Ortiz: anything in terms of licensing or escrow? procurement will ask about the source escrow in case of vendor exit.
[09:36] Jordan: we can discuss licensing. standard private contract includes an escrow option for critical binaries and artifacts; terms are negotiable and we'll put that in a POA.
[09:45] Markus Lee: ok, next practical step — hardware survey. we want redwood to tell us if our current nodes are sufficient or if we need to buy x more A100s.
[09:54] Maya: we'll run a sizing calc off your model family and typical concurrency. if you can share a representative prompt set and qps expectations, we'll output a recommended BOM.
[10:05] Jordan: i'll summarize next steps at the end but quick note — would you consider a short pilot? two-node dedicated cluster to validate the runbook?
[10:13] Dr. Lina Ortiz: yes a pilot is attractive if it maps to our validation gates and test cluster.
[10:18] Priya Shah: timeline — procurement would like all security docs within two weeks to start an MSA review.
[10:24] Jordan: we can get those to you. maya will hand off the runbook template and security whitepaper.
[10:30] Maya: final note — common pitfalls: not priming KV cache before traffic causing cold latency spikes; missing signature verification step; and insufficient test prompt coverage. we'll add those to the runbook.
[10:43] Jordan: okay, let me recap and we'll park Q&A after.
[10:47] Jordan: recap: 1) redwood provides signed bundles or reproducible manifests for you to sign; 2) we support HSM/PKCS#11 and local-only key ops; 3) we provide eval harness and smoke tests for offline validation; 4) canary rollouts and rollback tooling available; 5) local observability and immutable audit bundles; 6) optional escrow and licensing provisions.
[11:12] Dr. Lina Ortiz: that aligns with our needs. thanks, very helpful.
[11:17] Markus Lee: thank you. we'll schedule a hardware survey and share prompt set.
[11:22] Priya Shah: we'll start compliance review once we get the security docs.
[11:26] Jordan: great. we'll send the docs and runbook as promised and propose dates for the hardware survey. thanks everyone.
[11:34] End of meeting.
next_steps: Jordan to send private deployment runbook template and sanitized example within 3 business days
Maya to attach security whitepaper and HSM/KMS integration guide
Customer to provide representative prompt set and QPS expectations for sizing
Schedule on-site or remote hardware survey (propose dates in email thread)
